system_overview: This specification is a variant of the Simple algorithm from Lamport's 'Teaching Concurrency' that generalizes the shared registers from atomic to regular registers. Regular registers, as defined in Lamport's 1986 paper 'On Interprocess Communication' (Distributed Computing 1, 2, pp. 77-101), are weaker than atomic registers: a read that overlaps a write may return either the old value or the new value being written. This specification models regular register semantics by representing each register as a set of values, and proves that the correctness property (at least one process reads 1 after all terminate) still holds under this weaker memory model.
actors_and_components: The system consists of N processes, numbered 0 through N-1, arranged logically in a circle. Each process has a shared regular register that it writes to and that its right neighbor reads. The generalization to regular registers was proposed by Yuri Abraham in 'On Lamport's Teaching Concurrency' (Bulletin of EATCS No. 127, February 2019).
state_variables: The system tracks two arrays indexed by process number (0 through N-1): (1) a shared register array where each entry is a nonempty set of values from {0, 1}, representing the possible values a read might return from that regular register, and (2) a local read-result array where each process stores the value it obtained from reading its left neighbor's register (a single value, either 0 or 1). A program counter array tracks which of four steps each process is currently at.
initial_state: Each shared register is initialized to the singleton set {0} (representing a register whose value is definitely 0). All local read-results are initialized to 0. Every process begins at its first step.
actions: Each process executes three steps in sequence, modeling a regular register write as two substeps: (1) Begin-write step: the process changes its shared register from {0} to {0, 1}, representing the intermediate state where a concurrent read might see either the old value 0 or the new value 1. (2) Complete-write step: the process changes its register from {0, 1} to {1}, representing the completion of the write -- any subsequent read will now definitely see 1. (3) Read step: the process nondeterministically selects any value from the set currently in its left neighbor's register (at position (i-1) modulo N), stores that value as its local read-result, and terminates. After all processes terminate, a stuttering step prevents deadlock reporting.
safety_properties: The key correctness property is identical to the Simple specification: whenever all processes have terminated, at least one process must have read the value 1. The specification also includes a type-correctness invariant ensuring the register sets are nonempty subsets of {0, 1}, the read-results are in {0, 1}, and the program counters are in the expected set. An inductive invariant ensures that any process past the write-completion step has its register equal to {1}.
liveness_properties: Termination: eventually all processes reach the terminated state.
model_bounds: N (the number of processes) is a constant positive natural number. For model checking, N is set to a specific finite value.
additional_assumptions: The specification includes a complete formal machine-checked proof of the correctness property. The proof follows the same structure as the Simple proof but requires an additional decomposition step for the read action to handle the nondeterministic choice from the register set. Each local read-result variable is accessible only to its own process (it is local, not shared). The regular register model assumes single-writer registers -- each register is written by exactly one process.
